items.key: ai:so that's what burnhamism is all about
items.text: So that's what Burnhamism is all about
items.article: The Prime Minister revealed more about his approach to politics in an hour-long speech to the Labour Party on Tuesday. If you heard a faint fizzing sound around 2.30pm yesterday, it may have been your local economist popping open a celebratory bottle of Champagne. That was the moment Andy Burnham did something in his speech to Labour conference that, even 24 hours beforehand, felt politically impossible – he announced the end of the state pension triple lock . Actually, not even that. He signalled that Labour would put an adjustment to the triple lock in its party manifesto at the next election, with the savings going towards the cost of the planned National Care Service . It wouldn’t come into effect until April 2030. Currently, the annual rise in the state pension is decided by the highest figure out of 2.5%, the inflation rate, and wage growth. Under the change, the automatic link to wages would be dumped. So, the state pension would still rise by a minimum of 2.5% each year and more in times of high inflation. But it wouldn’t grow faster than earnings – which makes sense, economists argue, since it’s the taxes on those earnings that fund the state pension. There are arguments to be had over whether Burnham’s plan is the best possible solution to the triple lock quandary, and there’s already widespread scepticism of the suggestion that the savings would make much of a dent in the mammoth cost of a National Care Service.

items.text: My Patient Started Eating More Protein But Wasn’t Losing Weight. She Was Surprised When This 1 Particular Kind Made A Difference.
items.article: “At Diane’s next visit, I didn’t tell her to eat less. I told her to eat differently." Diane sat across from me looking like someone who’d done everything right and gotten nothing for it. She was 58, and she’d spent three months following the advice that’s everywhere right now. The headlines, the wellness accounts, this year’s new federal dietary guidelines, which single out women over 40 by name: Eat more protein. She’d taken it seriously, on her own initiative, before we’d ever discussed it — Greek yogurt at breakfast, a chicken breast at lunch, a protein shake most afternoons, salmon or steak most nights. She’d started lifting twice a week. She brought a food diary to the visit, unprompted, because she wanted me to see she wasn’t lying to either of us. Her weight hadn’t moved. Not up, not down. It was just stuck, in a way that made her start to wonder, quietly, whether something was actually wrong with her. I’m a physician-researcher. I run randomized clinical trials on diet and metabolic health, and I’d watched this same protein message spread through my patient population for months without ever pushing back on it. It’s advice I don’t think is wrong, exactly, in the broad strokes. But sitting across from Diane, watching her go through that food diary meal by meal, waiting for me to find the thing she’d done wrong, I realized that nobody had asked her a simple but impactful question: not how much protein are you eating, but where is it coming from?
